title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably mark short-answer responses in K-12 education, focusing on the educational assessment task rather than direct instructional use. The authors ask whether GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can classify student responses as correct or incorrect on open-response questions, and whether performance varies by subject, grade band, and item difficulty.

The study uses a newly assembled dataset of 1,710 student responses from the Carousel online quizzing platform, spanning Science and History questions across Key Stages 2, 3, and 4 (ages 5-16). Human expert teachers first rated the responses, establishing ground truth and interrater agreement, and then the same items were evaluated by LLM configurations using zero-shot and few-shot prompting. The comparison is direct but not an intervention study; it benchmarks model scoring against human raters.

Results show that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting performed best, reaching Cohen's kappa of 0.70, which was close to human agreement at 0.75. GPT-3.5 performed substantially worse (kappa 0.44-0.45), and few-shot prompting offered only a modest improvement. Performance was relatively stable across subjects, key stages, and question difficulty, suggesting potential utility for low-stakes formative assessment support in K-12 settings. The paper's strongest evidence is for GPT-4 as an automated scoring aid, while also highlighting that human agreement sets a practical ceiling for performance on ambiguous short-answer items.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for zero-shot and few-shot automated scoring/grading of short-answer student responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated whether GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-0125-preview could mark K-12 student short-answer responses as correct or incorrect, compared against expert human raters and the rater ground truth.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,710 short-answer responses from K-12 Science and History questions, GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved Cohen's kappa=0.70 against the expert-human ground truth, compared with human rater agreement of kappa=0.75. The paper reports this as close to human-level performance for automated marking.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human ground truth on correct/incorrect grading; Cohen's kappa

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3.5-turbo performed substantially worse than GPT-4 for the same grading task, with kappa=0.44 in zero-shot and 0.45 in few-shot conditions. The authors note the improvement was mainly due to GPT-4's much higher recall.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human ground truth on correct/incorrect grading; Cohen's kappa

quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational model-evaluation study, not an RCT or quasi-experiment on student learning outcomes. The paper does report clear quantitative agreement statistics, but the methodology concerns and absence of causal inference keep it below experimental tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported agreement for the best model is moderate-to-strong (kappa=0.70) and close to human raters, but the paper evaluates grading accuracy rather than instructional impact. That makes the educational impact indirect and not clearly tied to learning gains.
